title: Augustine and Pelagius
hook: can we be good without grace? Augustine said no; Pelagius was judged to say yes

segments.voice: Yesterday, original sin: Augustine said inherited guilt, the Orthodox said mortality and a wound. Your line was wounded, not worthless.

One short line in a prayer started a long quarrel. In his Confessions, Augustine says to God, more or less: give what you command, and then command whatever you will. If you want me to be good, you'll have to give me the goodness first. Augustine himself later wrote that a monk named Pelagius, said to have come from Britain, heard that line and couldn't stand it. To Pelagius it sounded like an excuse, as if people could sit back and wait for God to make them good. Their argument filled books. Today: Augustine and Pelagius.

The question underneath is simple to ask: can a person be good without grace? Grace, here, means God's help, freely given, not earned. Pelagius was a serious man who wanted Christians to live what they said they believed. God gave us free will and the commandments, he argued, and God doesn't command the impossible. So we can obey, and we're responsible when we don't. When he spoke of grace, he pointed to gifts already given: our nature, the law, the example of Jesus. Augustine saw a wound left untreated. In his reading, the human will itself is bent, and a bent will can't straighten itself any more than a broken leg can set itself. So grace has to come first, not as a reward for trying, but as the healing that makes trying possible. He leaned on Jesus's words in John's Gospel: "for without me ye can do nothing." Church councils sided with Augustine, and Pelagius's teaching was condemned. Some historians think Pelagius was more careful than his opponents made him sound, since some of his words reach us through their quotations: worth remembering whenever the winners of an argument describe the losers. And Paul gave both men a verse to hold. Philippians: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do." Churches still balance those two sentences differently. But the West's answer, after that long argument, was grace first.
screen: `WORK IT OUT; GOD WORKS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing waiting for you today that you'd rather avoid, a hard email, a dull chore, a conversation you've put off, and notice how much of you wants to do it well and how much doesn't. If you pray, you can ask God for help with that one task, by name. If you don't, notice that you won't do it entirely on your own: someone taught you, someone fed you, something got you this far.
Augustine and Pelagius. An old argument over whether people can be good without grace. Pelagius stressed our power to obey; Augustine said grace must come first.
Your line: grace first. The healing comes before the trying. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Western churches, Catholic and Protestant, teach that God's grace comes before any good a person does, following Augustine against Pelagius, and some Christians pray for help before beginning a task or a day's work.

notes: Augustine's prayer ('give what you command, and command what you will', Confessions 10.29/10.40) is paraphrased, not quoted. Pusey 1838 renders it close to 'give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt'; quote it only if a Keeper confirms the exact wording.
Pelagius's reaction to the line is reported by Augustine (On the Gift of Perseverance 20.53); attributed to Augustine in the script. Confirm reference.

'Said to have come from Britain': tradition and ancient opponents (e.g., Jerome) place his origin in Britain; confirm the hedge. Also confirm that some of Pelagius's words survive mainly in opponents' quotations (some of his own works survive, e.g., the Letter to Demetrias and the commentary on Paul).
'Church councils sided with Augustine, and Pelagius's teaching was condemned' (councils at Carthage and later Ephesus): no dates or counts given. Confirm.
Pelagius is presented fairly, as serious and possibly misrepresented; the index's 'was judged to say yes' is honored. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with the line about losing sides being painted.
The Orthodox East did not frame grace and free will in exactly Augustine's terms (synergy); howItsDone limits the Augustinian answer to Western churches. Confirm.
